e-564.knowledge_point: Finding the Time Intervals on which a Particle is Moving in a Particular Direction
e-564.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) = 3t^2+2t-6,$ where $t > 0$ is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle is stationary when $t=0\,\textrm s,$ determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving to the right.
e-564.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}+2t-6)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}+{t}^{2}-6t+C\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the particle is stationary at the time $t=0.$ This means $v(0) = 0,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =(0)^{3}+(0)^{2}-6(0)+C \\ 0 & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore the velocity of the particle is

$$
v(t) = t^3+t^2-6t.
$$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *right*, we must solve the inequality $v > 0.$ This gives

$$
t^3+t^2-6t = t(t+3)(t-2) > 0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t),$ we get the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14063912/assets/03b5ff6282d59038cbb355c0c3f017b544f286228ba4c3a82329897b4b43674c.png)

The particle moves to the right when $v(t)$ is positive. So, from the graph, we see that the particle moves to the right when $t>2.$

e-565.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity
e-565.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) = 6t-3t^2,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ when $t=1\,\textrm s,$ calculate the maximum velocity $v_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
e-565.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d t} = a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t) = 0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t) = 0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 6t-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 3t(2-t) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t> 0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t = 2\,\textrm s.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-3{t}^{2}) \\  & =6-6t \\ {v}^{″}(2) & =6-6(2) \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Since $v''(2) <      0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=2\,\textrm s.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6t-3{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}-{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1) = 2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3(1)^{2}-(1)^{3}+C & =2 \\ 3-1+C & =2\,⟹\,C=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) =3t^2-t^3.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
v_{\text{max}}= v(2) = 3(2)^2 - (2)^3 =4\,\textrm m / \textrm s
$$

So the maximum velocity $v_{\text{max}}=4\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ is reached at $t=2\,\textrm s.$

e-7226.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle is Stationary
e-7226.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\textrm m / \textrm s^2,$ given by the function $a(t) =2t-6$, where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=4\,\textrm m / \textrm s$ when $t=1\,\textrm s$, determine the moments in time when the particle is stationary.
e-7226.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\textrm m / \textrm s.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t-6)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}-6t+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1) =4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =(1)^{2}-6(1)+C \\ 4 & =-5+C \\ C & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t) = t^2-6t + 9.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\textrm m / \textrm s\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-6t+9 & =0 \\ (t-3)^{2} & =0 \\ t & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=3 \,\textrm s.$

before.html:
Question 2
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=1−2t, where t>0 is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle has velocity v=−6m/s when t=4s, determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the right.

a
 3<t<6
b
 t>3
c
 t>6
d
 2<t<4
e
 0<t<3
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating a(t)=1-2t gives v(t)=t-t^2+C. Using v(4)=-6 gives -12+C=-6, so C=6. Thus v(t)=t-t^2+6=(3-t)(t+2), which is positive for -2<t<3. Restricting to t>0, the particle moves right when 0<t<3.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=1-2t$, where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle has velocity $v=-6\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=4\,\text{s}$, determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the right.
after.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (1-2t)\text{d}t \\  & =t-{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(4)=-6.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =(4)-(4)^{2}+C \\ -6 & =4-16+C \\ -6 & =-12+C \\ C & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=-{t}^{2}+t+6.$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *right*, we must solve the inequality $v>0.$ This gives

$$
-{t}^{2}+t+6=-({t}^{2}-t-6)=-(t+2)(t-3)>0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t),$ we get the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14063912/assets/74db16dc00f5d08637cef02960409b7fd15c4bd3c19f577fa5a1f30ac8c402d3.png)

From the graph, we see that $v>0$ whenever $0<t<3.$

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, a(t)=2t−5, where t>0 is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle has velocity v=10m/s when t=6s, determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the left.

a
0<t<4
b
0<t<1
c
1<t<4
d
t>4
e
 t>1
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=t^2-5t+C. Since v(6)=10, 36-30+C=10, so C=4. Thus v(t)=(t-1)(t-4). The particle moves left when v(t)<0, which occurs exactly for 1<t<4.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ $a(t)=2t-5,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. after.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t-5)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}-5t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(6)=10.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =(6)^{2}-5(6)+C \\ 10 & =6+C \\ C & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{2}-5t+4.$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *left*, we must solve the inequality $v<0.$ This gives

$$
{t}^{2}-5t+4=(t-1)(t-4)<0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t)$, we get the following picture.

Question 3

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, a(t)=2t−5, where t>0 is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle has velocity v=10m/s when t=6s, determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the left.

a
0<t<4
b
0<t<1
c
1<t<4
d
t>4
e
 t>1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(2t−5)dt=t2−5t+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(6)=10. Substituting this into the above gives 10=(6)2−5(6)+C10=6+CC=4.

Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=t2−5t+4.

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the left, we must solve the inequality v<0. This gives

t2−5t+4=(t−1)(t−4)<0.

Plotting the graph of v(t), we get the following picture.

From the graph, we see that v<0 whenever 1<t<4.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Time Intervals on which a Particle is Moving in a Particular Direction
content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ $a(t)=2t-5,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. The positive direction is left to right. If the particle has velocity $v=10\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=6\,\text{s},$ determine the time intervals in which the particle moves to the left.
content.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t-5)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}-5t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(6)=10.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =(6)^{2}-5(6)+C \\ 10 & =6+C \\ C & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{2}-5t+4.$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *left*, we must solve the inequality $v<0.$ This gives

$$
{t}^{2}-5t+4=(t-1)(t-4)<0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t)$, we get the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14063912/assets/ad76f817f7c6e4a254e8881c34270eb875e72d821531566cb141cb393dcead72.png)

From the graph, we see that $v<0$ whenever $1<t<4.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}-6t-4)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-4t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =(4)^{3}-3(4)^{2}-4(4)+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-4t.$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *left*, we must solve the inequality $v<0.$ This gives

$$
{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-4t=t(t-4)(t+1)<0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t)$, we get the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14063912/assets/002f547b882940d087d6ed9d228334ec163931cfea0665eafdfe8b6ec8d863da.png)

From the graph, we see that $v<0$ whenever $0<t<4.$

Question 6
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=15−3t, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=14m/s when t=1s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

a
vmax=37.5m/s,t=5s
b
vmax=75m/s,t=5s
c
vmax=38m/s,t=5s
d
vmax=24.5m/s,t=2s
e
vmax=14m/s,t=1s
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=15t-(3/2)t^2+C. Using v(1)=14 yields C=1/2. Since v'(t)=15-3t is positive before t=5 and negative afterward, the maximum occurs at t=5 s. Its value is v(5)=75-37.5+0.5=38 m/s.

If the particle has velocity $v=14\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
after.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 15-3t & =0 \\ t & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=5\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(15-3t) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(5)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=5\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (15-3t)\text{d}t \\  & =15t-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=14.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}15(1)-\frac{3}{2}(1)^{2}+C & =14 \\ C & =\frac{3}{2}-1\,⟹\,C=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{1}{2}+15t-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(5)=\frac{1}{2}+15(5)-\frac{3}{2}(5)^{2}=38\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

after.html:
Question 6
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=15−3t, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=14m/s when t=1s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

a
vmax=37.5m/s,t=5s
b
vmax=75m/s,t=5s
c
vmax=38m/s,t=5s
d
vmax=24.5m/s,t=2s
e
vmax=14m/s,t=1s
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The extrema of the velocity v occur at the critical points of v.

Since dvdt=a(t), to find the times where v is a maximum, we just need to solve a(t)=0 and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving a(t)=0 gives

a(t)=015−3t=0t=5.

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when t=5s.

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of v(t): d2vdt2=ddt(dvdt)=ddt(a(t))=ddt(15−3t)=−3

Since v″(5)<0, we conclude that the velocity is maximized when t=5s.

Now, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(15−3t)dt=15t−32t2+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(1)=14. Substituting this into the above gives 15(1)−32(1)2+C=14C=32−1⟹C=12. Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=12+15t−32t2.

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

vmax=v(5)=12+15(5)−32(5)2=38m/s

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms v(t)=1/2+15t-(3/2)t^2=38-(3/2)(t-5)^2. Therefore the global maximum is 38 m/s at t=5 s, matching option c. Option a omits the integration constant 1/2.

before.html:
Question 7
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=2−23t, where t⩾0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=4m/s when t=0s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

a
vmax=13m/s,t=2s
b
vmax=4m/s,t=3s
c
vmax=7m/s,t=3s
d
vmax=203m/s,t=2s
e
vmax=293m/s,t=1s
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating acceleration and using v(0)=4 gives v(t)=4+2t-t^2/3=7-(t-3)^2/3. This reaches its global maximum of 7 m/s at t=3 s.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=2-\frac{2}{3}t,$ where $t⩾0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
after.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 2-\frac{2}{3}t & =0 \\ t & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=3\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-\frac{2}{3}t) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(3)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=3\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2-\frac{2}{3}t)\text{d}t \\  & =2t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2(0)-\frac{1}{3}(0)^{2}+C & =4 \\ 0+0+C & =4\,⟹\,C=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=2t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{2}+4.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(3)=2(3)-\frac{1}{3}(3)^{2}+4=7\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

Question 7
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=2−23t, where t⩾0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=4m/s when t=0s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

a
vmax=13m/s,t=2s
b
vmax=4m/s,t=3s
c
vmax=7m/s,t=3s
d
vmax=203m/s,t=2s
e
vmax=293m/s,t=1s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The extrema of the velocity v occur at the critical points of v.

Since dvdt=a(t), to find the times where v is a maximum, we just need to solve a(t)=0 and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving a(t)=0 gives

a(t)=02−23t=0t=3.

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when t=3s.

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of v(t) d2vdt2=ddt(dvdt)=ddt(a(t))=ddt(2−23t)=−23.

Since v″(3)<0, we conclude that the velocity is maximized when t=3s.

Now, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(2−23t)dt=2t−13t2+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(0)=4. Substituting this into the above gives 2(0)−13(0)2+C=40+0+C=4⟹C=4. Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=2t−13t2+4.

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

vmax=v(3)=2(3)−13(3)2+4=7m/s

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity
content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=2-\frac{2}{3}t,$ where $t⩾0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
content.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 2-\frac{2}{3}t & =0 \\ t & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=3\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-\frac{2}{3}t) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(3)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=3\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2-\frac{2}{3}t)\text{d}t \\  & =2t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2(0)-\frac{1}{3}(0)^{2}+C & =4 \\ 0+0+C & =4\,⟹\,C=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=2t-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{2}+4.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(3)=2(3)-\frac{1}{3}(3)^{2}+4=7\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$  

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & =0 \\ 5t & =\pi n \\ t & =\frac{\pi }{5}n,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer.  

Therefore, the extrema of the velocity function, for $t>0,$ are

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{5},\frac{2\pi }{5},\frac{3\pi }{5},…
$$

We now test the extrema values, starting with the least, using the second derivative test. For this, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)) \\  & =50\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).\end{aligned}
$$

At $t=\frac{\pi }{5},$ the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{5}) & =50\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\cdot \frac{\pi }{5}) \\  & =50\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =-50<0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{5})<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=\frac{\pi }{5}.$ Therefore, the first time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity is $t=\frac{\pi }{5}\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int 10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\text{d}t \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+C & =2 \\ -2+C & =2 \\ C & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$$
v(t)=4-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{\text{max}} & =v(\frac{\pi }{5}) \\  & =4-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\cdot \frac{\pi }{5}) \\  & =4-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =6\,\text{m}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the maximum velocity  ${v}_{\text{max}}=6\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached first time at  $t=\frac{\pi }{5}\,\text{s}.$

If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the earliest time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

The maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}=$
{{field-1}}
$\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached first time at $t=$
{{field-2}}$\text{s}.$
content.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$  

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & =0 \\ 5t & =\pi n \\ t & =\frac{\pi }{5}n,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer.  

Therefore, the extrema of the velocity function, for $t>0,$ are

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{5},\frac{2\pi }{5},\frac{3\pi }{5},…
$$

We now test the extrema values, starting with the least, using the second derivative test. For this, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)) \\  & =50\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).\end{aligned}
$$

At $t=\frac{\pi }{5},$ the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{5}) & =50\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\cdot \frac{\pi }{5}) \\  & =50\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =-50<0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{5})<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=\frac{\pi }{5}.$ Therefore, the first time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity is $t=\frac{\pi }{5}\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int 10\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\text{d}t \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+C & =2 \\ -2+C & =2 \\ C & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$$
v(t)=4-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{\text{max}} & =v(\frac{\pi }{5}) \\  & =4-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\cdot \frac{\pi }{5}) \\  & =4-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =6\,\text{m}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the maximum velocity  ${v}_{\text{max}}=6\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached first time at  $t=\frac{\pi }{5}\,\text{s}.$

before.html:
Question 10
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=16t−t3, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=44m/s when t=2s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

a
vmax=44m/s,t=2s
b
vmax=64m/s,t=4s
c
vmax=144m/s,t=4s
d
vmax=22m/s,t=1s
e
vmax=80m/s,t=4s
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=8t^2-t^4/4+C. Using v(2)=44 gives C=16. Acceleration t(16-t^2) is positive for 0<t<4 and negative for t>4, so velocity is maximized at t=4 s. Then v(4)=128-64+16=80 m/s.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=16t-{t}^{3},$ where $t>0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=44\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=2\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
after.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 16t-{t}^{3} & =0 \\ t(16-{t}^{2}) & =0 \\ t(4-t)(4+t) & =0 \\ t & =0,\pm 4.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=4\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(16t-{t}^{3}) \\  & =16-3{t}^{2} \\ {v}^{″}(4) & =16-3(4)^{2} \\  & =-32\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(4)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=4\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (16t-{t}^{3})\text{d}t \\  & =8{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(2)=44.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}8(2)^{2}-\frac{1}{4}(2)^{4}+C & =44 \\ 32-4+C & =44\,⟹\,C=16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=16+8{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{4}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(4)=16+8(4)^{2}-\frac{1}{4}(4)^{4}=80\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

Question 10
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=16t−t3, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=44m/s when t=2s, calculate the maximum velocity vmax of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

a
vmax=44m/s,t=2s
b
vmax=64m/s,t=4s
c
vmax=144m/s,t=4s
d
vmax=22m/s,t=1s
e
vmax=80m/s,t=4s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The extrema of the velocity v occur at the critical points of v.

Since dvdt=a(t), to find the times where v is a maximum, we just need to solve a(t)=0 and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving a(t)=0 gives

a(t)=016t−t3=0t(16−t2)=0t(4−t)(4+t)=0t=0,±4.

Since t>0, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when t=4s.

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of v(t) and evaluate it at t=4:

v″(t)=d2vdt2=ddt(dvdt)=ddt(a(t))=ddt(16t−t3)=16−3t2v″(4)=16−3(4)2=−32 Since v″(4)<0, we conclude that the velocity is maximized when t=4s.

Now, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(16t−t3)dt=8t2−14t4+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(2)=44. Substituting this into the above gives 8(2)2−14(2)4+C=4432−4+C=44⟹C=16.

Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=16+8t2−14t4.

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

vmax=v(4)=16+8(4)2−14(4)4=80m/s

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle Reaches Its Maximum Velocity
content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=16t-{t}^{3},$ where $t>0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=44\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=2\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
content.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 16t-{t}^{3} & =0 \\ t(16-{t}^{2}) & =0 \\ t(4-t)(4+t) & =0 \\ t & =0,\pm 4.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0$, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=4\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(t) & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(16t-{t}^{3}) \\  & =16-3{t}^{2} \\ {v}^{″}(4) & =16-3(4)^{2} \\  & =-32\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(4)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=4\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (16t-{t}^{3})\text{d}t \\  & =8{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(2)=44.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}8(2)^{2}-\frac{1}{4}(2)^{4}+C & =44 \\ 32-4+C & =44\,⟹\,C=16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=16+8{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{4}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(4)=16+8(4)^{2}-\frac{1}{4}(4)^{4}=80\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=(2/3)t^(3/2)-t^2/2+C. Since v(1)=1/6, C=0. For t>0, setting v(t)=t^(3/2)(2/3-sqrt(t)/2)=0 gives sqrt(t)=4/3, hence t=16/9 s.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=\sqrt{t}-t,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=\frac{1}{6}\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s},$ determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\sqrt{t}-t)\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=\frac{1}{6}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} & =\frac{2}{3}(1)^{3/2}-\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{6} & =\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{6} & =\frac{1}{6}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}=0 \\ 4{t}^{3/2}-3{t}^{2}=0 \\ {t}^{3/2}(4-3{t}^{1/2}) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,\frac{16}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=t−t, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=16m/s when t=1s, determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.

a
t=16s
b
t=16s
c
t=1s
d
t=43s
e
t=169s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The particle is stationary when v=0m/s.

First, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time: v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(t−t)dt=23t3/2−12t2+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(1)=16. Substituting this into the above gives 16=23(1)3/2−12(1)2+C16=23−12+C16=16+CC=0. Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=23t3/2−12t2.

Now, we find the moments in time when v=0m/s:

23t3/2−12t2=04t3/2−3t2=0t3/2(4−3t1/2)=0t=0,169

Since t>0, the particle is stationary when t=169s.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Times at Which a Particle is Stationary
content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=\sqrt{t}-t,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=\frac{1}{6}\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s},$ determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
content.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\sqrt{t}-t)\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=\frac{1}{6}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} & =\frac{2}{3}(1)^{3/2}-\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{6} & =\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{6} & =\frac{1}{6}+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2}-\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}=0 \\ 4{t}^{3/2}-3{t}^{2}=0 \\ {t}^{3/2}(4-3{t}^{1/2}) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,\frac{16}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t>0,$ the particle is stationary when $t=\frac{16}{9}\,\text{s}.$

decision.explanation: Integrating acceleration gives v(t)=sqrt(t)+C. Using v(9)=1 gives 3+C=1, so C=-2. The particle is stationary when sqrt(t)-2=0, hence t=4 s.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}},$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=1\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=9\,\text{s},$ determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(9)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\sqrt{9}+C \\ 1 & =3+C \\ C & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\sqrt{t}-2.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{t}-2 & =0 \\ \sqrt{t} & =2 \\ t & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=4\,\text{s}.$

Question 15

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=3t2−6t−4, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=30m/s when t=5s, determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.

a
t=0s
b
t=1s
c
t=4s
d
t=5s
e
t=2s
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives v(t)=t^3-3t^2-4t+C. Using v(5)=30 gives 125-75-20+C=30, so C=0. Thus v(t)=t(t-4)(t+1). Its only zero with t>0 is t=4 seconds.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=3{t}^{2}-6t-4,$ where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=30\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=5\,\text{s},$ determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.
after.worked_solution:
The particle is stationary when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}-6t-4)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-4t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(5)=30.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}30 & =(5)^{3}-3(5)^{2}-4(5)+C \\ 30 & =125-75-20+C \\ 30 & =30+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-4t.$

Now, we find the moments in time when $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-4t & =0 \\ t({t}^{2}-3t-4) & =0 \\ t(t-4)(t+1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $t=-1,0,4.$

Since $t>0,$ we discard solutions $t=-1,0.$ 
Therefore, the particle is stationary when $t=4\,\text{s}.$

Question 15
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration, measured in m/s2, given by the function a(t)=3t2−6t−4, where t>0 is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity v=30m/s when t=5s, determine the moment in time when the particle is stationary.

a
t=0s
b
t=1s
c
t=4s
d
t=5s
e
t=2s
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The particle is stationary when v=0m/s.

First, we find v(t) by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(3t2−6t−4)dt=t3−3t2−4t+C To determine C, we use the fact that v(5)=30. Substituting this into the above gives 30=(5)3−3(5)2−4(5)+C30=125−75−20+C30=30+CC=0. Therefore, the velocity v of the particle at time t is v(t)=t3−3t2−4t.

Now, we find the moments in time when v=0m/s:

t3−3t2−4t=0t(t2−3t−4)=0t(t−4)(t+1)=0

The solutions are t=−1,0,4.

Since t>0, we discard solutions t=−1,0. Therefore, the particle is stationary when t=4s.
